To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effect of resolving a sub-clinual uterine infection in early lactation has no effect on plasma and follicle fluid steroid concentrations at the time when cows are rebred.
resolving a subclinical endometritis in early lactation does not change the steroid profile in follicular fluid and plasma at the time of ovulation in dairy cows.
In early lactation dairy cattle, resolving a sub-clininal uterine infection does not affect plasma or follicular fluid steroid profiles at the time of first ovulation after calving.

the impact of subclinical endometritis (scendo) on the ovarian follicular dynamics and steroid concentrations in early postpartum dairy cows.
the effect of subclinical endometritis (scendo) in early lactating dairy cows on ovarian follicle dynamics.
the impact of subclinical endometritis on ovarian follicle dynamics and steroid concentrations, and the effects of resolving the infection on these parameters.

there is no effect of resolving a sub-clinically infected uterus on steroid concentrations at the time when rebreeding is attempted in dairy cows.
resolving sub-clinical endo in dairy cows does not alter the steroid profile of the follicular fluid or plasma in early lactation.
resolving scEndo does not affect plasma or FF oestrogen and progestagen concentrations in early lactating dairy cattle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

scEndo in lactating dairy cows has a negative effect on ovarian function, and that this effect is not resolved until a significant proportion of the infection has resolved, and that this is not reflected in plasma or FF steroid profiles.
resolving scEndo does not alter plasma and FF oestradiol, androstenedione, progesterone, cortisol, and corticosterone concentrations at the time cows are rebred.

cows with sub-clinical endo-metritis (scEM), which is common in the dairy industry, do not show any changes in the concentrations of oestrogen, progesterone, androgens or cortisol in their follicular fluid (ff), when they resolve the infection.
